rationale: Both legs are the same underlying construct (low cash / low liquidity slack — note RANK(capx/che) is dominated by the inverse of the cash balance), so the "interaction" is largely a double-count of the cash-holdings/financial-constraint dimension and is a component-level recombination of two archived signals rather than a new mechanism; the declared interaction_type "ratio" also does not match the rank-product expression.

target_name: Escalating Capex Into Deterioration, Rank Product
rationale: This is the archived "Escalating Capex Into Deteriorating Profitability" with one leg's ZSCORE(RANK(.)) stripped to RANK(.) — an explicitly cosmetic operator variant with identical economics, and the operator-vs-mechanism lesson it claims to isolate is not worth a full slot.

A legitimate and cheap test of whether the investment–distress relation is monotone or U-shaped, and the expression matches the hypothesis, but be aware the first leg runs directly against the well-documented asset-growth anomaly (low asset growth predicts *higher* returns), so a negative slope would have to overcome a strong known force and a null result will be hard to interpret.

target_name: Inventory Growth Financed by Deteriorating Current Position
rationale: Replacing the level of working capital with the year-over-year change in the current-liability-to-current-asset ratio is a substantive, well-motivated response to the mechanical-overlap critique and identifies the financing source rather than the accounting footprint; residual concern is that inventory sits in the denominator of the conditioner, which mechanically pushes the two legs in opposite directions.

The tax-shield framing is appealing and the data item is new to the archive, but txt/at is close to a monotone transform of pretax profitability, so the expression computes "high investment × low profitability" — the q-theory investment/profitability interaction already probed by two archived signals — meaning the stated mechanism is not what the signal identifies.

A genuinely different, well-argued construction of a populated long leg (self-funded investment) rather than the CMA-loading low-investment definition that failed twice, though the second leg alone is close to the published net-debt-issuance/change-in-leverage anomaly and high capex mechanically inflates the asset denominator of lt/at, so part of the interaction may be accounting rather than economic.
